tier_reason: Upgraded from B to A on stronger evidence. Boost.JSON's own Benchmarks page compares against RapidJSON (pool and CRT allocators) and nlohmann/json. It states the CPU (Intel Core i7-7700K @ 4.20GHz, Windows 10, 32GB), the compilers and flags (gcc 8.1 -O3, clang 12.0 -O3, msvc 19.26 /O2), and the method. The benchmark code is public at boostorg/json bench/bench.cpp, with raw data in bench/results.txt and bench/samples.txt. The originally cited danielaparker/json_benchmarks pages would only be C: that suite has 6 stars, is run by the jsoncons author, and states no CPU model.

corrections.workload: Boost.JSON's own bench program (bench/bench.cpp) measures in-memory parse and serialize throughput in MB/s over 14 standard JSON files between 64KB and 3.25MB: apache_builds, canada, citm_catalog, github_events, gsoc-2018, instruments, marine_ik, mesh, mesh.pretty, numbers, random, twitter, twitterescaped and update-center. It compares boost (default allocator) and boost (pool/monotonic_resource) against rapidjson (CrtAllocator), rapidjson (MemoryPoolAllocator) and nlohmann/json. Each configuration runs for at least 5 s per sample, and the median samples are averaged.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Page charts, in MB/s, listed as clang / gcc / msvc. Parse citm_catalog: boost 476/503/477 vs nlohmann 140/143/148 (~3.3-3.5x, derived from page data), and boost(pool) 1120/1096/999 vs rapidjson(pool) 1200/1279/978, so it is slower on clang and gcc and roughly tied on msvc. Parse canada: boost 385/395/369 vs nlohmann 55/26/52 (~7-15x, derived from page data), and boost(pool) 642/675/637 vs rapidjson(pool) 506/641/490. Serialize citm_catalog: boost 2882/3263/2128 vs nlohmann 1151/1204/1142 (~1.9-2.7x, derived from page data) and vs rapidjson 2210/2469/2135. Across all 14 files x 3 compilers (derived from page data / bench/results.txt): boost beats nlohmann in 42/42 parse cases (2.1x-38.7x, median ~2.6x) and 42/42 serialize cases (1.7x-9.3x, median ~3.5x). Against RapidJSON, boost (default) wins only 20/42 parse cases (median ~0.94x); boost(pool) beats rapidjson(pool) in 33/42 parse cases (median ~1.26x); boost beats rapidjson in 33/42 serialize cases (median ~1.17x).
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-7700K CPU @ 4.20GHz, Windows 10, 32GB RAM
corrections.caveats: These are first-party results, last regenerated on 2020-10-21 (commit 8f42799) and not re-run since; bench/bench.cpp has changed since then (2025 commits). The RapidJSON and nlohmann versions are unpinned (bench/clone.sh does a depth-1 clone of HEAD) and are not stated on the page. The clear win is over nlohmann/json; against RapidJSON the result is mixed, and Boost.JSON loses several parse workloads (e.g. random.json, citm_catalog and twitter on gcc). Independent corroboration comes from danielaparker/json_benchmarks (VS 2022 17.14.16 /O2 /Ot, Boost 1_90, laptop with no CPU model, run by the jsoncons author, single run, timing includes file stream I/O). There Boost.JSON reads the 540.82MB integer file in 2.269s vs nlohmann 8.177s and RapidJSON 2.254s, and the 794.72MB float file in 3.579s vs 15.997s and 3.443s.

notes: I switched benchmark_url to the project's own A-grade page. The numbers from the original json_benchmarks pages were all accurate for the Boost.JSON row and are kept in caveats as corroboration. The default branch is develop; its latest commit is dated 2026-09-23 (committer date), while pushed_at of 2026-09-24 reflects another branch. 479 stars and BSL-1.0 are confirmed.

tier_reason: The numbers come from the project author's own benchmark repo; its README says it exists 'to measure how jsoncons compares to other json libraries'. It is first-party and neither well-known nor independent (6 stars). The code is public (src/tests/*_benchmark.cpp, src/test_driver.cpp), and the compiler (VS 2022 17.14.16) and flags (/O2,/Ot) are stated, but there is no CPU model, only 'Windows, Intel' and the laptop model. That makes it first-party and short of A, so C, not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Integer file (540.82MB): jsoncons reads in 3.918s and writes in 0.744s vs nlohmann 8.177s / 2.885s (~2.1x read, ~3.9x write faster, derived from page data). Against RapidJSON (2.254s / 0.656s) jsoncons is slower on both read and write (derived from page data). Float file (794.72MB): jsoncons 8.879s / 3.879s vs nlohmann 15.997s / 7.165s (~1.8x faster both ways, derived from page data). Against RapidJSON (3.443s / 3.061s) jsoncons is slower on both (derived from page data).
corrections.hardware: Page lists 'Lenovo Thinkpad X Extreme with 8 cores, 16 hardware threads, 32 GB memory, 2 TB solid state drive'; Environment 'Windows, Intel'; OS given as 'Windows 2011'. No CPU model stated.
corrections.caveats: This is a first-party shootout run by the jsoncons author: a single run on a single machine with no CPU model. The timed read and write include std::ifstream / std::ofstream I/O. jsoncons beats nlohmann (and jsoncpp and reflect-cpp) but is slower on read than yyjson, RapidJSON, Boost.JSON and glaze, and slower on write than yyjson, Boost.JSON and RapidJSON. The float-file page prints the jsoncons version as an unexpanded macro string; the integer page says 1.8.1. The independent miloyip/nativejson-benchmark (2016, clang 7.0, i7-4980HQ) showed mixed results against nlohmann for old versions: slower on canada parse (77.3 vs 55.6 ms), faster on twitter parse (3.5 vs 7.0 ms).

notes: Every number matches the jsoncons rows on the two report pages (report updated 2026-07-03). GitHub license spdx is NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is the Boost Software License 1.0 text, so BSL-1.0 and copyable stand. The star count (853) and last commit (2026-09-22) are confirmed.

tier_reason: The README Benchmarks section is first-party and compares directly against encoding/json. The benchmark code is public (parser_timing_test.go, validate_timing_test.go) and Go 1.12 is stated, but the only hardware given is goos linux / goarch amd64, with no CPU model. That makes it C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'up to 15x faster than the standard encoding/json'. Parse vs stdjson-map (decode into map[string]interface{}): citm_catalog 918.87 vs 62.19 MB/s (~14.8x), canada 538.22 vs 33.03 MB/s (~16.3x), twitter 815.86 vs 55.94 MB/s (~14.6x) (derived from page data). Parse vs the faster stdjson-struct / stdjson-empty-struct modes: citm 918.87 vs 115.64 MB/s (~7.9x), canada 538.22 vs 127.11 MB/s (~4.2x), twitter 815.86 vs 110.05 MB/s (~7.4x) (derived from page data). Validation: citm_catalog 1025.39 vs 237.48 MB/s (~4.3x), canada 757.07 vs 265.74 MB/s (~2.8x), small 493.60 vs 198.83 MB/s (~2.5x) (derived from page data).
corrections.hardware: linux/amd64 (goos/goarch only); CPU model not stated
corrections.caveats: The README numbers date from 2019 (Go 1.12, README benchmark commit 2019-03-09) and have not been re-run on modern Go, whose encoding/json has improved since. There is no CPU model, and this is a first-party benchmark only. The ~15x headline is against decoding into map[string]interface{}; against struct or empty-struct decoding the gap is ~4-8x, and for validation ~2.5-4.3x. fastjson does not materialize Go values, and parsed objects must be released before the next Parse.

notes: Every quoted number appears verbatim in the README; I only added derived-ratio markers and context. MIT license, 2468 stars, not archived, not a fork, and last commit 2026-02-21 (active) are all confirmed. This is a Go library, so it is in scope only if the list accepts non-C++ entries.
